lead: A straight beam bends into a smooth curve called the elastic curve. At every section, the curvature of this curve equals the bending moment divided by EI, where E is Young's modulus and I is the second moment of area. This link turns a strength problem into a deflection problem. Designers use it to keep floors, bridges and machine shafts within serviceability limits, for example a 4 m floor beam that must not sag more than span/250. This chapter sets up the differential equation; the next chapters solve it.
prereq: You need Unit 3 (shear force and bending moment diagrams) and Unit 4 (bending stress and EI); after this chapter, 5.2 Double integration method integrates the equation.

blocks.text: Take x along the beam axis from a chosen origin, in metres. Take y as the vertical deflection, positive upward. A loaded beam bends into a smooth curve y(x) called the elastic curve. The quantity EI is the flexural rigidity: E is Young's modulus in kN/m² (or N/m²), and I is the second moment of area in m⁴. EI has units kN·m².

Curvature measures how sharply the curve turns. It is κ = 1/R, where R is the radius of curvature in metres, so κ has units 1/m. For small slopes, κ ≈ d²y/dx². The theory of simple bending from Unit 4 gives M/I = E/R, so 1/R = M/EI.

blocks.where: E is Young's modulus; I is the second moment of area; y is deflection positive upward; x is distance along the beam; M(x) is the bending moment at x, positive sagging.

blocks.text: Sign convention: y upward and sagging M positive. A sagging beam is concave up, so d²y/dx² is positive and EI y″ = M. If you take y downward while keeping sagging M positive, the same physical sag gives negative d²y/dx², so the equation becomes EI y″ = −M. Write your convention at the top of every answer.

sections.h3: The governing equation and boundary conditions

blocks.text: EI d²y/dx² = M(x) is called the governing differential equation of the elastic curve, or the equation of the elastic curve. It is second order, so two boundary conditions fix the solution. Do not integrate here; 5.2 Double integration method does that.
Differentiate once: EI y‴ = V, where V is shear force. Differentiate twice: EI y⁗ = −w, where w is the downward distributed load per unit length. These follow from dM/dx = V and dV/dx = −w.

head: Support
Conditions
rows: Free end (no concentrated load applied there)
M = 0 so y″ = 0; V = 0 so y‴ = 0. If a point load P acts at the free end, V = P instead.

blocks.text: The figure shows the chain: load integrates to shear, shear to moment, moment divided by EI gives curvature, curvature integrates to slope, slope to deflection. A mistake in any link, especially the sign of M, changes the whole chain.

sections.h3: How to set up the equation

items: Choose x from one end and state the range, for example 0 ≤ x ≤ 4 m.
Choose y positive upward or downward. Write the sign convention before any equation.
Find support reactions from equilibrium, as in Unit 3.
Write M(x) from the bending moment diagram. Sagging positive.
Write EI y″ = M(x). Use EI y″ = −M(x) if y is downward.
List boundary conditions from the table.
Check units: M in kN·m and EI in kN·m² give y″ in 1/m.

blocks.text: For a simply supported beam with UDL w over span L, the reactions are wL/2 each. With x from the left support, M(x) = (wL/2)x − wx²/2. Sagging is positive. This is the setup used in the example below.

A cantilever fixed at x = 0 with a downward point load P at the free end x = L has M(x) = −P(L − x). The negative sign means hogging. At the fixed end, y = 0 and y′ = 0. At the free end, M = 0, so y″ = 0. The shear at the free end equals the load applied there, V = P (not zero), so y‴ = P/EI. Use y‴ = 0 at a free end only when no concentrated load acts at that end.

figure.caption: Load integrates to shear and moment, moment divided by EI gives curvature, and curvature integrates to slope and deflection. Notice curvature M/EI is the hinge of the chain.

spec.title: From load to deflection
spec.aria: A block diagram runs from load to shear to moment to curvature, then integrates curvature to slope and slope to deflection.

examples.question: A simply supported beam of span 4 m carries a uniformly distributed load of 6 kN/m over the whole span. EI = 5000 kN·m². Take x from the left support, y positive upward, and sagging bending moment positive. (a) Write M(x) for 0 ≤ x ≤ 4 m. (b) Find the curvature at midspan.
steps: Total load = 6 kN/m × 4 m = 24 kN. By symmetry, each reaction is 12 kN.
Cut the beam at distance x from the left support. The left part has upward reaction 12 kN and downward UDL of 6x kN acting at x/2 from the cut.
Curvature = M/EI = 12 / 5000 = 0.0024 m⁻¹. Positive means concave up, consistent with sagging.
examples.answer: M(x) = 12x − 3x² kN·m and the curvature at midspan is 0.0024 m⁻¹.
examples.check:
L = 4.0
w = 6.0
EI = 5000.0
R = w*L/2
x = L/2
M = R*x - w*x**2/2
curv = M/EI
print(R)
print(M)
print(curv)

traps: Mixing sign conventions: a sagging moment with y downward needs EI y″ = −M. Write the convention at the top of every answer.
Confusing curvature with radius of curvature. Curvature is κ = 1/R = M/EI; the radius is R = EI/M. A large radius means slight bending, not sharp bending.
Using EI in N·m² with M in kN·m without converting. Keep kN and metres together, or convert both.
Taking M(x) from the wrong end or with the wrong sign. Match the bending moment diagram from Unit 3.
Treating the small-deflection equation as exact for large sag. It assumes slopes are small.

quiz.q: State the governing differential equation of the elastic curve when y is positive upward and sagging moment is positive.
quiz.a: EI d²y/dx² = M(x), where M is positive sagging.

quiz.q: Why does a sagging moment give positive d²y/dx² when y is upward?
quiz.a: A sagging beam is concave up. With y upward, concave up means the slope increases with x, so d²y/dx² is positive.

quiz.q: A simply supported beam has M(x) = 12x − 3x² kN·m and EI = 5000 kN·m². Find the curvature at x = 1 m.
A student uses y downward but keeps EI y″ = M with M sagging positive. What sign error appears in the deflection?
quiz.a: The equation should be EI y″ = −M. Using +M reverses the curvature sign, so the computed deflection comes out upward instead of downward.

quiz.q: List the boundary conditions at a fixed end and at a simple support.
quiz.a: Fixed end: y = 0 and y′ = 0. Simple support: y = 0 and M = 0, so y″ = 0.

quiz.q: Explain why EI y⁗ = −w for a downward distributed load w.
quiz.a: Differentiate EI y″ = M to get EI y‴ = V, then EI y⁗ = dV/dx. For downward w, dV/dx = −w, so EI y⁗ = −w.

quiz.q: For a beam segment whose bending moment is M(x) = −10x kN·m with EI = 2000 kN·m², find y″ at x = 2 m.
The example beam has curvature 0.0024 m⁻¹ at midspan. What is the radius of curvature there, and what does the sign mean?
quiz.a: R = 1/κ = 1/0.0024 ≈ 417 m. Positive curvature means concave up, consistent with sagging.

beyond: Not for the exam. Large deflections need the elastica equation, where curvature is written as y″/(1+y′²)^{3/2} and the equation becomes nonlinear. Finite element programs use beam elements based on this chapter's equation, often adding shear deformation in Timoshenko beams. Search 'Euler-Bernoulli beam equation' and 'elastica large deflection' to go further.
